title: Why Use Stochastic?
description: Compute [probability distributions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_probability_distributions) directly in DuckDB SQL — [PDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Probability_density_function), [CDF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cumulative_distribution_function), [quantile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quantile_function), [hazard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Failure_rate), and random sampling for 22 named distributions, all under a uniform `dist_<family>_<op>` naming scheme. Built for Monte Carlo sketches, what-if analysis, and synthetic data generation without leaving SQL.

sections.title: What this extension is for
sections.description: A complete statistical-distributions library exposed as scalar SQL functions. Best fit: ad-hoc analysis, [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method) sketches, [synthetic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data), p-values, and inline statistical math next to your warehouse data.

bulletPoints.label: Monte Carlo and what-if analysis
bulletPoints.description: Combine sampling functions with [`range()`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/functions/nested.html), aggregate the draws with regular SQL — no Python, no DataFrame round-trip.

bulletPoints.label: Synthetic data generation
bulletPoints.description: Populate test fixtures or anonymized columns with realistic distributions in a single [`CREATE TABLE AS`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table). Mix heights, counts, and wait times from different families in one query.

bulletPoints.label: Inline statistical math
bulletPoints.description: Compute [Z-scores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_score), p-values, [Value at Risk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_at_risk), or Bayesian credible intervals as plain SQL expressions wherever a value is allowed.

bulletPoints.label: Distribution properties as functions
bulletPoints.description: Mean, median, variance, skewness, kurtosis, support range — every property is a function (not a constant), so it composes inline.

sections.title: How it works
sections.description: The extension wraps the [Boost.Math statistical-distributions library](https://www.boost.org/doc/libs/release/libs/math/doc/html/dist.html) — the same battle-tested implementations used across C++ statistics tooling. Each of 22 distributions exposes the same 21-operation surface, generated from a single template.

bulletPoints.label: Uniform `dist_<family>_<op>` naming
bulletPoints.description: Every function is named for its distribution and operation. Operations include `sample`, `pdf`, `cdf`, `quantile`, `hazard`, the moments (`mean`, `variance`, `skewness`, `kurtosis`), and log-scale variants for likelihoods and tail probabilities.

bulletPoints.label: Vectorized over columns
bulletPoints.description: All functions are scalar — they run column-at-a-time over DuckDB's columnar engine. A million calls inside a `SELECT` is one vectorized scan, not a Python loop.

bulletPoints.label: Strict parameter validation
bulletPoints.description: Illegal parameters raise a SQL error rather than silently returning NaN, so typos in long pipelines fail fast instead of quietly poisoning downstream values.

sections.title: Scope and honest caveats
sections.description: A deep distributions library, but intentionally not a full simulation framework.

bulletPoints.label: Univariate only
bulletPoints.description: No [copula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copula_(probability_theory)) or multivariate-normal sampler. For correlated draws, sample independently and apply a [Cholesky-style transform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cholesky_decomposition) yourself.

bulletPoints.label: RNG seeding is not user-controlled
bulletPoints.description: There is no documented per-query seed. For exactly-reproducible runs, generate the draws once into a table and treat that table as the seed.

bulletPoints.label: No fitting or inference helpers
bulletPoints.description: One-way: parameters → distribution. No MLE / method-of-moments fitters, no built-in tests. Compute the test statistic in SQL and call the appropriate CDF complement for the p-value.

bulletPoints.label: Production simulations may want a notebook
bulletPoints.description: For large-scale agent-based simulation, MCMC, or [SciPy](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/stats.html)-grade fitting, keep a Python notebook. Stochastic shines for analyses that live next to warehouse data.

useCases.title: Monte Carlo over warehouse data
useCases.description: Wrap sampling functions in a CTE over `range(N)` and aggregate with SQL — estimate π, integrate a payoff function, run a [VaR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_at_risk) calculation against live position data, all without leaving the warehouse.

useCases.title: Generate realistic synthetic data
useCases.description: Build a fixture table with one [`CREATE TABLE AS`](https://duckdb.org/docs/sql/statements/create_table): heights from a Normal, session counts from a Poisson, conversion flags from a Bernoulli. Hundreds of thousands of rows in one query.

useCases.title: Inline p-values and confidence intervals
useCases.description: Compute a Z-statistic in SQL, then call the Normal CDF complement for the two-sided p-value. Same shape works for chi-squared, t, and other tests — analytics dashboards with first-class statistics.

useCases.title: Bayesian conjugate updates
useCases.description: Beta-Binomial, Gamma-Poisson, Normal-Normal — closed-form posteriors are one quantile call away. Useful for A/B-test dashboards and conversion-rate experiments.
